title: Eric Trump Predicts COVID-19 Would Vanish After the Election
description_short: On Fox News, Eric Trump said Democrats were exploiting the COVID-19 crisis and predicted it would disappear after the November election.
description_medium: Eric Trump told Fox News host Jeanine Pirro that Democrats were exploiting the COVID-19 crisis and predicted the coronavirus would “magically” disappear after November 3. Media Matters dates the broadcast to May 16, 2020; Fox News published its article just after midnight on May 17. The dates refer to the broadcast and the article publication.
description_long: In a May 16, 2020 appearance on Fox News’s Justice with Judge Jeanine, Eric Trump said Democrats were trying to exploit the coronavirus crisis to damage his father’s reelection campaign. He predicted that after November 3 the coronavirus would “magically all of a sudden go away and disappear” and the country would reopen. Fox News published its account at 12:13 a.m. Eastern on May 17 and quoted the interview. Media Matters identifies the segment as the May 16 edition of the program, while The Washington Post also reported the comments on May 17. The dates describe the broadcast and the following day’s news coverage. Eric Trump made the remarks during the 2020 presidential campaign, when his father was seeking reelection. The reports document what Eric Trump said; they do not establish his prediction about the virus or his account of Democrats’ motives as fact.

description_long: The EPA’s administrative docket for The GEO Group, Inc. lists a Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act complaint filed in June 2024 and a withdrawal filing in June 2025. ProPublica reported that the case concerned GEO Group’s use of the disinfectant Halt at its Adelanto, California, immigration detention facility. According to the EPA complaint as summarized in that report, GEO employees used the product without the protective equipment required by its label on more than 1,000 occasions in 2022 and 2023; these were agency allegations, not findings established in the withdrawn case. The EPA docket lists the complaint as withdrawn and closed, while ProPublica reported that the withdrawal notice gave no explanation. GEO Group’s political contributions and lobbying may be relevant context, but the available record does not establish that they caused the EPA’s action or that the company received a favor in exchange.

title: Lyn Redwood Presents Thimerosal Claims to CDC Vaccine Advisers
description_short: Former Children’s Health Defense president Lyn Redwood presented thimerosal claims to CDC vaccine advisers in June 2025.
description_medium: In June 2025, CNN reported that Lyn Redwood, a former president of Children’s Health Defense, was scheduled to present about thimerosal to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices. She presented at the June 26 meeting. CNN said one citation appeared to reference a study reporters could not locate, and CDC scientists challenged vaccine-safety presentations. Separate reports said HHS hired her for vaccine-safety work but did not identify her formal title. The original slur and specific-office claim are unsupported.
description_long: At a June 26, 2025 meeting of the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), Lyn Redwood presented claims about the vaccine preservative thimerosal. CNN and NBC News identified Redwood as a former president of Children’s Health Defense, an organization founded by Robert F. Kennedy Jr. CNN reported that she argued thimerosal was linked to autism and other harms and that one reference in her presentation appeared to point to a study reporters could not locate. CDC scientists publicly challenged vaccine-safety presentations at the same meeting. Separate CNN and CBS reports said HHS had hired Redwood for work connected to CDC vaccine safety but did not identify a formal public job title. These reports describe what was presented and how journalists and officials discussed it; they do not establish that ACIP or CDC adopted the claims as policy or that the presentation constituted a scientific finding. Redwood’s former role at Children’s Health Defense and the reported HHS work are distinct from her appearance before the advisory committee.
subcategory: Vaccine safety staffing and advisory meetings

title: Trump Signs Executive Order Targeting NPR and PBS Funding
description_short: Trump signed an order directing agencies and CPB to end NPR and PBS funding where the law allows.
description_medium: On May 1, 2025, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14290, directing federal agencies and the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to stop funding NPR and PBS where legally permitted. The order announced a funding directive; the available sources do not establish that payments were actually withheld from either broadcaster.
description_long: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14290, “Ending Taxpayer Subsidization of Biased Media,” on May 1, 2025. The order directed federal agencies to end direct or indirect funding for NPR and PBS to the extent permitted by law. It also directed the Corporation for Public Broadcasting to cease funding those outlets where consistent with its legal obligations. The order described the policy as ending taxpayer support for what it characterized as biased media. Its provisions set instructions for government agencies and CPB; they do not by themselves establish that NPR or PBS actually lost particular payments. The Federal Register published the order on May 7, 2025, and the White House posted its text. The directive was expressly limited by existing law and did not erase the statutory framework governing public broadcasting. It was a signed funding policy directed at the two broadcasters, not proof of a completed reduction in their revenue.

description_short: A February 2026 NPR investigation, summarized by PBS, reported that DOJ withheld portions of Epstein records mentioning Trump; allegations remain unverified.

Host Geoff Bennett said the material included allegations of sexual abuse of a minor and that some pages mentioning Trump had been removed from the public record. The segment does not independently establish the underlying allegation, confirm a count of withheld files, or explain DOJ’s reason for withholding them. It documents the investigation and the unresolved claims it reported.

title: Trump’s January 2017 Travel Order Led to Airport Detentions and Court Challenges
description_short: Executive Order 13769 restricted entry from seven countries; airport detentions prompted emergency court action, and Trump fired Acting Attorney General Sally Yates.
description_medium: President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769 on January 27, 2017, restricting entry from seven predominantly Muslim countries for 90 days and suspending refugee admissions. AP reported airport detentions and a judge’s emergency order barring deportation of covered travelers. DOJ records say Sally Yates directed lawyers not to defend the order; Trump fired her, and DOJ later reversed the instruction.
description_long: On January 27, 2017, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 13769, which suspended refugee admissions and restricted entry for 90 days for nationals of seven predominantly Muslim countries. The order took effect amid reports of airport detentions. The Associated Press reported that a federal judge temporarily barred deportation of travelers covered by the ban, while the ACLU described specific travelers detained at Logan Airport. Acting Attorney General Sally Yates instructed Justice Department attorneys not to present arguments defending the order because she was not convinced it was lawful. Trump dismissed Yates, and Deputy Attorney General Dana Boente later directed DOJ to defend the order. These events document the policy’s immediate airport and legal consequences. The cited reporting concerns specific travelers and does not establish that every affected traveler, including every green-card holder, was detained or deported. Later nationwide litigation and the subsequent revised order are outside this account’s scope.

title: Trump Grants Thomas K. Ford a Full and Unconditional Pardon
description_short: A DOJ warrant records Trump’s full pardon of Thomas K. Ford for 2003 federal convictions involving safety standards and false statements.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s pardon warrant records that President Donald Trump granted Thomas K. Ford a full and unconditional pardon. It identifies a Southern District of Illinois case and convictions under federal statutes concerning mandatory safety standards and false material statements, with a 2003 sentence of probation, a $2,000 fine, and a $125 assessment. The warrant does not explain the underlying conduct or Trump’s reasons.
description_long: The Justice Department’s recipient-specific pardon warrant identifies Thomas K. Ford and states that President Donald Trump granted him a full and unconditional pardon. The warrant lists a case in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Illinois and convictions under federal provisions concerning mandatory safety standards and false material statements or representations. It records that Ford was sentenced on April 10, 2003, to three years of probation, a $2,000 fine, and a $125 special assessment. The department’s pardon index also lists Ford among recipients of Trump’s clemency. These records establish the pardon and the sentence listed in the warrant, but they do not describe the underlying incident in detail or state why Trump granted clemency. The available recipient-specific record supports a factual account of the pardon without characterizing it as corrupt or assigning a rationale that the documents do not give.

title: FTC Sought Civil Action Over Trump’s Holiday and Bally Stock Acquisitions
description_short: At the FTC’s request, DOJ filed a 1988 civil case over Trump’s stock acquisitions in Holiday and Bally; Trump settled for a $750,000 civil penalty.
description_medium: The FTC’s case record says it asked the Justice Department to file a civil complaint after Donald Trump acquired stock in Holiday Corporation and Bally Manufacturing without timely premerger notifications. In April 1988, Trump agreed to settle the federal charges and pay a $750,000 civil penalty. The record concerns civil reporting requirements, not a criminal prosecution.
description_long: The Federal Trade Commission’s case file says the agency asked the Department of Justice to bring a civil case against Donald Trump over premerger-notification requirements. The 1988 complaint concerned stock acquisitions in Holiday Corporation and Bally Manufacturing through Bear Stearns. The government alleged that Trump acquired shares above the Hart–Scott–Rodino Act’s reporting threshold without submitting the required notices on time. In an April 5, 1988 release, the FTC said Trump agreed to settle the charges and pay a $750,000 civil penalty; the federal judgment entered that penalty. The case record identifies a civil complaint, settlement, and monetary judgment. It concerns federal reporting requirements for acquisitions, not a criminal prosecution or criminal conviction. The premerger filing system gives federal antitrust agencies notice of acquisitions so they can review potential effects on competition before closing. The FTC and court records establish the terms of the civil resolution and distinguish the complaint’s allegations from the settled outcome.

title: Wisconsin GOP Said It Trained More Than 5,000 Election Observers for 2024
description_short: Reuters reported that the RNC and Wisconsin Republican Party said they trained more than 5,000 election observers in Wisconsin.
description_medium: Reuters reported on October 31, 2024, that the Republican National Committee and Republican Party of Wisconsin said they had trained more than 5,000 election observers in the state. The report also described separate grassroots groups planning to deploy observers and monitor ballot drop boxes. It does not establish that Trump personally directed the training or that the program was a statewide voter-intimidation operation.
description_long: In an October 31, 2024 report about election observers in Wisconsin, Reuters said the Republican National Committee and Republican Party of Wisconsin reported training more than 5,000 observers. The article separately described grassroots groups that planned to deploy up to 1,500 observers collectively at voting sites and count centers and to monitor ballot drop boxes. It also reported local election officials’ concerns about observer conduct during earlier absentee-ballot processing in Milwaukee-area communities. Those facts support reporting on party training and local organizing, with attribution to the groups and officials. They do not show that Donald Trump personally deployed the observers, establish a nationwide strategy, or prove that all observers engaged in intimidation. The original headline combined separate actors and allegations into one claim that the source does not establish. This account focuses on the verifiable training statement and attributes separate deployment plans without treating them as completed activity.
